1ycck9r:612: The core engineering insight in the article is the strict separation of Skill and Config. A Skill is a self-contained workflow that includes System Prompts defining "what to do," MCP connectors defining "which systems can be operated," and configuration that drives triggers and behavior. Once a Skill is written, it can run permanently without requiring manual invocation each time. Config, by contrast, is a YAML file containing concrete business parameters: prepaid GL account codes, supplier code mapping tables, materiality thresholds, period-end partial month conventions, and routing rules (who gets called in which channel). When business rules change, you only edit the Config file without touching the Skill itself. The author notes this was a mistake he made before—cramming everything into one Prompt or one Skill file, so every business change required updating the entire Skill, leading to high maintenance costs and preventing reuse across scenarios. After separation, a Skill can be shared across multiple reconciliation entities (Entity/Entity groups) by simply swapping the Config file. This follows the same principle as separating configuration from logic in software engineering and is highly similar to the traditional finance IT approach of separating the chart of accounts from accounting logic. From an architectural perspective, this design decouples the AI Agent's capability boundary (Skill) from its business context (Config), allowing the same Skill to be deployed across different accounting entities, accounting standards, or organizational units—simply by providing the corresponding Config file. This greatly improves system scalability.
1yciirp:509: The article's human-AI collaboration design deserves special attention. After the AI Agent completes its work, it does not automatically post the JE; instead, it retains two manual control nodes: a human Preparer and a human Reviewer. The specific flow is: after completion, the Agent generates a summary (including workpaper, JE CSV, and the Preparer flag) and posts it to Slack. The Preparer manages the Agent, fixes errors/flags marked by the Agent, and performs a first-pass review. The Reviewer then executes the existing review procedures, serving as the final control node and sign-off. When the Agent flags issues requiring manual handling, the Preparer has two response options: (1) open the workpaper and manually fix the issue, then reply with a ✅ signal in Slack to notify the Agent to re-read the file and update; or (2) if the issue is likely to recur, directly update the Skill or Config file so it is handled automatically in the next cycle. This design creates a positive feedback loop of continuous improvement—manual fixes are converted into automated rules. This design reflects a deep understanding of the accounting profession: multi-layer review in the closing process is not a burden but an inherent mechanism to prevent error propagation. The AI Agent is positioned as a "super assistant" rather than a "replacement," freeing humans from repetitive operations and letting them focus on judgment and review.

hvhks8:29: 2. MCP as an Operating-System-Level Connection Protocol for AI Agents
kj53uj:427: The article repeatedly emphasizes that "MCP is the biggest unlock." MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard protocol that lets AI Agents plug into various software systems (Deel, NetSuite, Google Drive, etc.) to read data, execute actions, and take action on behalf of users within those systems. The author's core insight is that many companies still treat AI as a simple chatbot. But without system-level visibility, AI cannot do truly end-to-end work. AI needs to "see" the full context and be able to take action—even read-only action—to be genuinely useful. In the specific implementation, the author's prepaid expense Agent connects directly to the ERP GL module via MCP, eliminating manual CSV export/import. Workpapers are connected via MCP to Google Drive—the Agent reads last month's workpaper, creates new files, and writes the current month's prepaid additions and amortization data, all automatically.
